featureObjective: Implement a secure, lightweight internal system health status check endpoint for automated monitoring tools that provides reliable service liveness/uptime signals without exposing sensitive operational details.
userStory: As a platform reliability engineer, I want an internal health status endpoint that monitoring tools can poll so that we can rapidly detect service outages, verify availability after deployments, and trigger alerts without disclosing infrastructure internals.
businessRules: The endpoint must be read-only and support only HTTP GET.
The endpoint must be intended for internal or controlled monitoring usage; public unauthenticated internet access should be disallowed by default environment/network policy.
The response contract must be stable and version-safe for monitoring integrations (fields cannot be removed without a deprecation window).
The endpoint must not call downstream dependencies (database, cache, third-party APIs) to remain lightweight and avoid cascading failure amplification.
The endpoint must return process-level health only (service is running and responsive), not deep dependency health.
The endpoint behavior must be identical across staging and production except for environment metadata values.
Any failure in endpoint execution must fail safely by returning a generic error payload without implementation details.
No sensitive runtime values (hostnames, IPs, secrets, tokens, connection strings) may be included in response payloads or error bodies.
acceptanceCriteria: Given the service is running, when a GET request is sent to /internal/health, then the API responds with HTTP 200 and JSON payload containing at minimum: status='ok', service name, and uptime in seconds as a non-negative number.
Given uptime is reported, when parsed by monitoring tools, then the uptime field is always numeric, monotonic for a single process lifetime, and never negative.
Given an undefined nested route (e.g., /internal/health/extra or /internal/unknown/path), when requested, then the API returns the platform-standard HTTP 404 response format used by the service.
Given an unsupported HTTP method (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) on /internal/health, then the API returns HTTP 405 (or service standard method-not-allowed behavior) without side effects.
Given malformed headers or query parameters, when request validation fails, then the API still does not expose stack traces and returns standardized client error responses.

Given the endpoint is polled continuously, when 100 requests per second are sent for 5 minutes in a non-production performance environment, then p95 latency remains within the agreed NFR threshold and no memory leak trend is observed.
Given a request includes a correlation/request ID header, when logged, then the same ID is present in structured logs for observability.
Given the service starts successfully, when /internal/health is called, then uptime starts near zero and increases over time until process restart.

Given any unhandled internal exception occurs during endpoint processing, when response is sent, then client receives a generic error body with no raw stack trace and monitoring can still distinguish non-200 status.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Security: No raw infrastructure, runtime, framework, or database stack traces are exposed to clients under any circumstance.
Security: Response payload must exclude sensitive data (secrets, credentials, private hostnames, internal IPs, environment variable dumps).
Performance: Endpoint must be lightweight with no database/network I/O and target p95 latency <= 50 ms under normal internal load.
Reliability: Endpoint availability must match core service availability; if process is alive and request pipeline is healthy, endpoint returns 200 consistently.
Observability: Access and error logs for this endpoint must be structured, include timestamp, route, status code, latency, and correlation ID when available.
Maintainability: Health response schema should be explicitly typed/validated in code to prevent accidental contract drift.
Compatibility: Response must use application/json and remain backward compatible for monitoring clients across minor releases.
Compliance: Implementation must conform to the organization's API error handling and secure coding standards.
outOfScope: Deep dependency health checks (database connectivity, queue lag, third-party API reachability).
Readiness/liveness orchestration semantics beyond this single internal status endpoint (unless separately specified).
Authentication/authorization platform redesign; only endpoint-level integration with existing controls is expected.
Building a full monitoring dashboard or alert routing system.
Auto-remediation workflows triggered from health check failures.
Exposing operational diagnostics intended only for internal debugging to external clients.
